newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria finally gets the privatisation bug.
newsitem.headline: Algeria finally gets the privatisation bug.

text.p: Algeria expects to speed up its privatisation process after June parliamentary elections that are part of the government's programme to stabilise the oil and gas producing country.

"The privatisation process will go smoothly during the last quarter of 1997 but the privatisation will be speeded up in 1998," the privatisation council head Abderrahmane Mebtoul told Reuters on Sunday.
Officials in Algeria agree that privatisation will inject badly-needed technology, capital and market-oriented management.

Earlier this month, Algeria adopted a new privatisation law to woo investors to buy into state-owned firms. The legislation altered the landmark 1995 privatisation law to allow incentives to investors who save jobs and upgrade the firms they acquire.
The incentives include tax deductions and easy loans. The law changed the prior provisions that new owners keep on all workers and keep the firm's activity unchanged for five years.
The government will start off by offering about 250 state-owned firms and industrial units for sale in the upcoming months, Mebtoul said.
"These firms set for privatisation will enable us to test the process but I think the great launching will be in 1998," he added.
"The privatisation potential is huge because we have concentrated the investement in the state-owned economy since the independence of the country in 1962," he said.
Foreigner investors, including Germans, Portuguese and Spanish, have shown interest in buying into state-owned industry like cement works, vehicle and glass-making plants, he added.
"The foreigners are waiting impatiently for a legitimate government from the next elections," he said.

Algeria has been without an elected parliament since 1992 when the authorities scrapped a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead. Since then about 60,000 people have died in violence between Islamist rebels and government forces.
The authorities are pinning hope on the June 5 parliamentary elections to complete the structures of a legitimate government after presidential polls in 1995.
Mebtoul noted that President Liamine Zeroual had given clear signals the privatisation process had to be speeded up and industry made more efficient.
The main opposition parties competing in the upcoming parliament were business-oriented, including the Islamist Hamas group and its secularist foes, he said.
But Algeria had to keep up efforts to stabilise the macro- economic framework to improve the economy fundamentals to help the privatisation succeed, he said.
